{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=PCFG-derived+uncertainty+metrics+as+triggers+for+meta-reasoning+loops+in+AI+architectures&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1007/bfb0013954\", \"title\": [\"Reasoning with uncertainty in AI\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/bfb0013954\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1996]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-94-017-1743-4_3\", \"title\": [\"Temporal Semantics of Meta-Level Architectures for Dynamic Control of Reasoning\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-017-1743-4_3\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2001]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6759126\", \"title\": [\"An Engineering Framework for Self-Correcting Autonomous AI Agents: Mitigating Hallucinations and Reasoning Loops in Autonomous Engineering Workflows\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This paper presents TRACE (Trajectory Reliability and Correction Engine), a runtime self-correction framework for autonomous AI agents in engineering workflows. TRACE targets a reliability gap in multi-step tool-using agents, where unsupported claims, contradictions, repetitive loops, and tool-use anomalies can propagate across long execution trajectories. Existing self-correction methods typically rely on post-hoc reflection or a single intervention mechanism, but do not integrate continuous runtime monitoring, failure attribution, and adaptive recovery in one control layer. TRACE wraps a standard ReAct-style agent with four modules: a Trajectory Monitor, a Failure Attribution module, a Recovery Controller, and an Audit Layer for structured trace logging. We evaluate TRACE on a simulated enterprise incident-triage benchmark of 50 tasks with injected hallucination- and loop-inducing conditions across four difficulty levels. TRACE achieves 76.0% task success versus 68.0% for a self-reflection baseline and 62.0% for vanilla ReAct, while reducing hallucination incidence from 19.4% to 9.6% and loop frequency from 12.1% to 4.8%. The framework is intended for reliable, auditable autonomous execution in engineering environments.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6759126\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.5226493\", \"title\": [\"Synthetic reasoning - Designing AI Architectures Beyond N…

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=theoretical+scalability+constraints+of+curiosity-driven+developmental+AI+in+unstructured+problem+spaces&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.55640/ijaair-v03i08-12\", \"title\": [\"Scalability Constraints in AI-Driven Construction Management: Opportunities for Robotics and LLM Integration\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The increasing digitization of construction management has created opportunities for artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, cloud architectures, and large language models (LLMs) to support planning, coordination, monitoring, and operational decision-making. However, scalability remains a fundamental challenge because construction environments are characterized by heterogeneous workflows, distributed information, changing operational conditions, and uneven levels of technological adoption. This research and review paper examines the principal scalability constraints affecting AI-driven construction management and investigates how robotics and LLM integration can address selected operational and informational limitations. The study adopts a conceptual qualitative methodology based on grounded-theory principles, systematic interpretation of the provided literature, and cross-domain synthesis. The analysis identifies four interconnected scalability dimensions: technological infrastructure, organizational routines, human-system interaction, and learning and decision-support capacity. Cloud-oriented architectures provide a foundation for distributed computational access, while research on learning systems indicates that sustained technology adoption depends on perceived usefulness, quality, task value, and user capability. Grounded-theory studies further indicate that organizational routines and methodological processes influence how emerging technologies become embedded in operational practice. Within this framework, robotics can extend AI from informational decision support toward physical execution, whereas LLMs can improve the accessibility, interpretation, and coordination of heterogeneous construction information.
